unit-alg-t3-06.title: Topic 3 · 3-6 Theorems About Roots of Polynomial Equations
unit-alg-t3-06.srcName: enVision Algebra 2, Lesson 3-6 (Drive — the two Lesson 3-6 HW sheets, plus the vocabulary sheet and key)
unit-alg-t3-06.source: enVision Algebra 2 Lesson 3-6: Theorems About Roots of Polynomial Equations

summary.text: Lesson 3-6 covers the theorems that let you find every root of a polynomial: the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra (exactly n roots), the Rational Root Theorem (a finite list of candidates), and the Complex and Irrational Conjugate Theorems (awkward roots always come in pairs).

why.text: This is the lesson that finishes the job Lesson 3-5 started. Factoring finds the easy roots; these theorems find the rest, and tell you when to stop looking.

objectives.text: State how many roots a polynomial has, counting multiplicity
List the possible rational roots using the Rational Root Theorem
Use the Complex and Irrational Conjugate Theorems to name paired roots
Combine testing, division and the Quadratic Formula to find every root

parentNote.text:
A note on sources: her Topic 3 folder has no student-edition file for 3-6 the way it does for the other six lessons — this one is covered instead by the two “Lesson 3-6 HW” PDFs, and those are what this unit is built from, alongside the 3-6 vocabulary sheet and its answer key.

Worth knowing about that homework: roughly a quarter of it is WORD PROBLEMS — a closet, a safe, a fish tank, a cost function — where a volume or a total is given and the dimensions have to come back out of a polynomial. Those are the questions that look least like the rest of the lesson and are the easiest to be caught out by, so this unit covers them directly, including the two steps most often dropped: substituting x back to get the actual dimensions rather than stopping at x, and discarding the roots a length cannot be. Her homework also lists rational-root candidates for polynomials with leading coefficients of 2, 4 and 8, where the candidates are genuinely fractions — so the unit asks for one of those rather than an easier leading coefficient of 1, which hides the whole difficulty.

The distinction most worth reinforcing is what each theorem promises: the Fundamental Theorem guarantees the COUNT, while the Rational Root Theorem only supplies a list to try — and a polynomial can easily have no rational roots at all. The other reliable trap is the conjugate: only ONE sign flips, the one on the imaginary part or the radical.

nextUp.text: Work one quartic all the way through — candidates, divide, divide, then the Quadratic Formula.

cards.def:
**A polynomial of degree n has exactly n roots, counting multiplicity, if complex roots are allowed.**
• “Exactly”, not “at most” — the count is only guaranteed once imaginary numbers are on the table.
• A cubic always has 3 roots; some may be repeated and some may be complex, but there are always 3.
cards.hint: Count in the complex numbers and the answer is always exactly the degree.

cards.def:
**Over the REAL numbers a degree-n polynomial has AT MOST n roots; over the complex numbers it has EXACTLY n.**
• x² + 1 has no real roots but two complex ones, i and −i.
• The graph only shows the real ones — a complex root is never an x-intercept.
cards.hint: The graph shows real roots only. The rest are invisible on it.

cards.def:
**Any rational root is ±p⁄q, where p divides the constant term and q divides the leading coefficient.**
• It gives a finite LIST OF CANDIDATES to test — it does not say any of them actually work.
• For 2x³ + x − 6: p ∈ {1,2,3,6}, q ∈ {1,2}, so candidates are ±1, ±2, ±3, ±6, ±½, ±3⁄2.
cards.hint: p from the constant, q from the leading coefficient. Constant on top.

cards.def:
**Substitute it, or synthetic-divide by it — a zero result means you have found a root AND a factor.**
• Synthetic division is usually better: it confirms the root and hands you the quotient at the same time.
• The quotient is one degree lower, so the problem shrinks every time a root is found.
cards.hint: Each root found makes the next one easier — the polynomial gets smaller.

cards.def:
**If a + bi is a root of a polynomial with real coefficients, then a − bi is a root too.**
• Complex roots always arrive in PAIRS.
• So a polynomial with real coefficients always has an EVEN number of complex roots — which is why every odd-degree polynomial must have at least one real root.
cards.eq: a + bi is a root ⇒ a − bi is a root
cards.hint: Complex roots come two at a time, never alone.

cards.def:
**If a + √b is a root of a polynomial with RATIONAL coefficients, then a − √b is a root too.**
• The same pairing rule as complex roots, for irrational ones.
• So finding 2 + √5 as a root tells you 2 − √5 is one as well, for free.
cards.eq: a + √b is a root ⇒ a − √b is a root
cards.hint: Surds pair up too, for the same reason complex roots do.

cards.def:
**Because the coefficients are real, anything irrational or imaginary has to cancel out when the factors are multiplied.**
• (x − (2 + i))(x − (2 − i)) = x² − 4x + 5 — every trace of i is gone.
• Only the pair multiplies to something with real coefficients, which is why one can never appear without the other.
cards.hint: The pair multiplies to a real quadratic. A lone one never could.

cards.term: The strategy for finding every root
cards.def:
**List candidates, test until one works, divide it out, then solve what is left.**
• Rational Root Theorem for the list; synthetic division to test and to shrink.
• Once the quotient is a QUADRATIC, stop hunting — factor it or use the Quadratic Formula, which finds complex roots too.
cards.hint: Hunt only until the leftover is a quadratic. Then use a formula.

cards.term: What the theorems do and do not promise
cards.def:
**The Fundamental Theorem guarantees the COUNT; the Rational Root Theorem only offers a list to try.**
• A polynomial can easily have no rational roots at all — the candidate list can come up empty-handed.
• Knowing there are exactly n roots does not tell you what any of them are.
cards.hint: One theorem counts; the other suggests. Neither hands you an answer.

cards.term: Example: finding every root of a cubic
cards.def:
**x³ − 2x² + x − 2 has roots 2, i and −i.**
• Candidates from the Rational Root Theorem: ±1, ±2. Testing 2 gives zero.
• Dividing by (x − 2) leaves x² + 1, whose roots are i and −i — a conjugate pair, as required.
• Three roots for a cubic, exactly as the Fundamental Theorem promises.
cards.hint: One rational root, then a quadratic. That is the usual shape of these.

cards.term: Using roots to find a dimension
cards.def:
**When a volume is given and the sides are expressions in x, multiply them out, set the result equal to the volume, and solve the polynomial.**
• A box measuring x by x + 2 by x − 1 with volume 140 gives x³ + x² − 2x = 140, so P(x) = x³ + x² − 2x − 140 = 0.
• Everything must be on one side before the Rational Root Theorem or the Zero Product Property can be used — that subtraction is a step, not a formality.
cards.hint: Multiply first, move the volume across second, hunt roots third.

cards.term: x is not the answer — the dimensions are
cards.def:
**Solving gives you x; the sides are what the expressions equal once x is put back in.**
• x = 5 in a box measuring x by x + 2 by x − 1 means 5 by 7 by 4, not 5.
• Check by multiplying the three back together — it costs a moment and catches an arithmetic slip immediately.
cards.hint: Solve for x, then substitute. Stopping at x answers a question nobody asked.

cards.term: Throw away the roots a length cannot be
cards.def:
**A measurement has to be real and positive, so negative and non-real roots are rejected — even though they genuinely solve the equation.**
• A cubic from a volume problem usually has one usable root and two that are non-real.
• If the leftover quadratic has a negative discriminant, its two roots are non-real, which is how you know the real one you found is the only one to consider.
cards.hint: The algebra offers three answers. The box accepts one.

questions.q: How many roots does a degree-5 polynomial have, counting multiplicity and allowing complex roots?
opts: Exactly 5
At most 5
At least 5
It depends on the coefficients
questions.hint: The Fundamental Theorem of Algebra is an exact count, not a bound.
steps: The Fundamental Theorem of Algebra gives the count over the complex numbers.
A degree-n polynomial has exactly n roots there, counting multiplicity.
Here n = 5.
So exactly 5.

ex.main: **Exactly 5.** "At most" is the right phrasing for REAL roots only — over the complex numbers the count is exact and never depends on the coefficients. That precision is what makes the theorem useful: you always know how many roots you are still looking for.
ex.tip: Real roots: at most n. All roots: exactly n. The word changes with the number system.

questions.q: Which list gives every possible RATIONAL root of 0 = 2x³ − 5x² − x + 6?
questions.hint: Factors of the constant on top, factors of the leading coefficient underneath. A leading 2 means halves.
steps: The constant is 6, so p comes from 1, 2, 3 and 6.
The leading coefficient is 2, so q comes from 1 and 2.
Dividing each p by each q gives ±1, ±2, ±3, ±6 and the halves ±½ and ±³⁄₂.
(6⁄2 and 2⁄2 repeat 3 and 1, so they add nothing new.)

ex.main: **±1, ±2, ±3, ±6, ±½ and ±³⁄₂.** Stopping at the whole numbers is the commonest way to miss a root outright — and here it would, because ³⁄₂ really is a root of this polynomial. A leading coefficient of 1 is the only case where every candidate is a whole number, which is exactly why an example with one teaches nothing about the hard part.
ex.tip: Leading coefficient 1 → whole numbers only. Anything else → expect fractions, and write them down.

questions.q: If 3 + 2i is a root of a polynomial with real coefficients, what else must be a root?
questions.hint: A conjugate flips the sign of the imaginary part only.
steps: The Complex Conjugate Theorem says roots come in conjugate pairs.
The conjugate of a + bi is a − bi.
Here a = 3 and b = 2.
So 3 − 2i must also be a root.

ex.main: **3 − 2i.** Only the imaginary part changes sign — the real part stays exactly as it is. Negating both (−3 − 2i) or swapping the numbers around (2 + 3i) are the two near-misses, and neither is the conjugate.
ex.tip: Conjugate: same real part, opposite imaginary part. Nothing else moves.

questions.q: If 1 + √7 is a root of a polynomial with rational coefficients, what else must be a root?
questions.hint: Irrational roots pair the same way complex ones do.
steps: The Irrational Conjugate Theorem applies when the coefficients are rational.
The conjugate of a + √b is a − √b.
Here a = 1 and √b = √7.
So 1 − √7 is also a root.

ex.main: **1 − √7.** Only the sign in front of the radical flips. It is the same idea as complex conjugates and for the same underlying reason: only the pair multiplies back to something with rational coefficients.
ex.tip: Both conjugate theorems flip exactly one sign — the one on the "awkward" part.

questions.q: What does the Rational Root Theorem actually guarantee?
opts: Any rational root there is will appear in the list
At least one of the candidates is bound to be a root
Every candidate on the list turns out to be a root
The polynomial has no irrational roots to worry about
questions.hint: It narrows the search; it does not promise a find.
steps: The theorem says where rational roots CAN be.
So a rational root, if one exists, is somewhere in the list.
It never promises the list contains an actual root — a polynomial may have none that are rational.
So: any rational root will appear in the list.

ex.main: **Any rational root will appear in the candidate list.** It is a filter, not a finder. x² − 2 has candidates ±1 and ±2 and neither works, because its real roots are ±√2 — irrational, and completely outside what this theorem can see.
ex.tip: It shrinks an infinite search to a finite one. That is the whole contribution.

questions.q: A polynomial with real coefficients has degree 3 and one root equal to 2i. What are its other roots?
opts: −2i and another complex root
−2i and one real root
Two more complex roots
2i again, with multiplicity 3
questions.hint: Count what the Fundamental Theorem requires, then apply the pairing rule.
steps: Degree 3 means exactly 3 roots.
2i is a root, so its conjugate −2i must be too — that is 2 roots.
The third cannot be complex, because complex roots pair up and there is no partner left.
So the third root is real: −2i and one real root.

ex.main: **−2i and one real root.** Complex roots always come in pairs, so an odd-degree polynomial with real coefficients must have at least one real root — there is no way to pair up an odd number. That is why every cubic graph crosses the x-axis somewhere.
ex.tip: Odd degree with real coefficients always has a real root. The ends run opposite ways, so it has to cross.

questions.q: For P(x) = 2x³ − 5x² + x + 2, which is a candidate the Rational Root Theorem allows but ±4 is not?
opts: ¼
½
⅔
questions.hint: Build the candidate list from the constant and the leading coefficient.
steps: The constant is 2, so p ∈ {1, 2}.
The leading coefficient is 2, so q ∈ {1, 2}.
Candidates are ±1, ±2 and ±½.
½ is allowed; 4, ¼ and ⅔ all involve numbers that are not factors of 2.

ex.main: **½.** Fractional candidates arise exactly when the leading coefficient is not 1, and both parts have to be legitimate factors: 1 divides the constant and 2 divides the leading coefficient. ¼ would need a 4 in the denominator, and ⅔ a 3 — neither divides 2.
ex.tip: A leading coefficient of 1 means the candidates are all whole numbers. Anything else opens up fractions.

questions.q: Find all roots of x³ − 6x² + 11x − 6.
opts: 1 and 6
1, 2 and 6
1, 2 and 3
questions.hint: Test the small candidates first — they are the likeliest.
steps: Candidates are ±1, ±2, ±3, ±6.
Dividing by (x − 1) leaves x² − 5x + 6.
That factors as (x − 2)(x − 3), so the roots are 1, 2 and 3.

ex.main: **1, 2 and 3.** One rational root found by testing turns the cubic into a quadratic, and the quadratic finishes by ordinary factoring. Note the roots are positive even though the constant is −6 — the signs of the roots are not read off the constant directly.
ex.tip: Test 1 and −1 first. They are quick to evaluate and often work.

questions.q: A degree-4 polynomial with real coefficients has roots 1 + i and 3. How many roots are still unaccounted for, and what do you know about them?
opts: One, and it must be real — 1 − i is already forced by the pairing
Two, and both of them are bound to be non-real numbers
Three, and every one of them has to be a real number
None — all four roots are already named or forced
questions.hint: Apply the pairing rule before you count. It supplies a root the question never listed.
steps: Degree 4 means exactly four roots, counting multiplicity.
1 + i is non-real, so its conjugate 1 − i is forced — the two given roots really account for three.
That leaves exactly one root unaccounted for.
A lone non-real root would need a partner, and there is no room left — so the fourth root is real.

ex.main: **One, and it has to be real.** Naming 1 + i quietly names 1 − i as well, so two stated roots account for three. The last one cannot be non-real: that would demand a conjugate partner, and a degree-4 polynomial has no fifth slot to put one in. Which real number it is stays open — it could even be 3 over again.
ex.tip: The pairing rule does two jobs: it adds roots you were not given, and it forces the odd one out to be real.

questions.q: Why must every polynomial of ODD degree with real coefficients have at least one real root?
opts: Because an odd-degree polynomial has no complex roots at all
Non-real roots come in pairs, so an odd count cannot all be non-real
Because the Rational Root Theorem always turns one of them up
Because an odd function always passes through the origin
questions.hint: Count parity: complex roots arrive two at a time.
steps: An odd-degree polynomial has an odd number of roots in total.
Complex roots always come in conjugate pairs, so they contribute an EVEN number.
An even number can never account for an odd total.
So at least one root must be real.

ex.main: **Complex roots come in pairs, so an odd number of roots cannot all be complex.** It is a pure parity argument and needs no computation at all. The graph says the same thing a different way: odd degree means the ends run opposite directions, so the curve has to cross the axis somewhere.
ex.tip: Two independent arguments — parity of the root count, and the end behaviour — reach the same conclusion.

questions.q: How many REAL roots and how many non-real roots does x⁴ − 1 have?
opts: 0 real and 4 non-real
4 real and 0 non-real
2 real and 2 non-real
3 real and 1 non-real
questions.hint: Factor it completely and read off what each factor contributes.
steps: x² − 1 = (x − 1)(x + 1), giving the real roots 1 and −1.
x² + 1 = 0 gives x = ±i, two non-real roots.
So 2 real and 2 non-real — four altogether, as degree 4 requires.

ex.main: **2 real and 2 non-real.** The Fundamental Theorem guarantees four roots in total; the graph shows only the two real ones as x-intercepts. And the non-real pair is exactly that — a pair — which is what the Complex Conjugate Theorem requires. The "3 real and 1 non-real" option is impossible for that reason alone.
ex.tip: A split with an ODD number of non-real roots is impossible when the coefficients are real.

questions.q: You are finding all roots of a quartic. You find one rational root and divide it out, leaving a cubic; you find another and divide again, leaving a quadratic. What now?
opts: Start again, because the division must have gone wrong somewhere
Keep testing rational candidates until two more of them work
Conclude that the two remaining roots must be irrational
Solve the quadratic directly — the formula finds complex roots too
questions.hint: Ask what tool finishes a quadratic completely.
steps: A quadratic can always be solved outright, by factoring or by the Quadratic Formula.
The Quadratic Formula finds the roots whatever they are — rational, irrational or complex.
So no more candidate-testing is needed.
Solve the quadratic directly.

ex.main: **Solve the quadratic directly.** The candidate-testing is only there to get you DOWN to a quadratic — once you are there, a formula finishes it for certain. Carrying on testing would be slow and could fail entirely, since the last two roots may be irrational or complex and no rational candidate would ever match them.
ex.tip: Hunt down to degree 2, then stop hunting. That is the whole method.

questions.q: What does the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra actually guarantee?
opts: Every polynomial of degree 1 or more has at least one complex root
Every polynomial of degree n has exactly n real roots
Every polynomial can be factored using only rational numbers
Every polynomial with real coefficients has at least one real root
questions.hint: Remember that every real number is also a complex number — the word is not a promise of an i.
steps: The theorem is about existence: a non-constant polynomial always has a root somewhere.
That root is guaranteed only in the COMPLEX numbers, which include the real ones.
Applying it repeatedly is what gives exactly n roots counting multiplicity.
So the guarantee is at least one complex root for any degree of 1 or more.

ex.main: **At least one complex root, for any degree of 1 or more.** Applying it over and over — root, divide out, root again — is what builds up to exactly n roots counting multiplicity. Guaranteeing a REAL root is a different and weaker claim that only holds for odd degree; x² + 1 has no real root at all and is the standard counterexample.
ex.tip: Complex includes real. The theorem promises a root, not a real one.

questions.q: For P(x) = 3x³ + x − 10, the Rational Root Theorem builds its candidates from which two numbers?
opts: Factors of 3 on top, factors of 10 underneath
Factors of 10 on top, factors of 3 underneath
Factors of 10 on top, factors of 1 underneath
Factors of 1 on top, factors of 10 underneath
questions.hint: p over q — and p is the end of the polynomial furthest from the leading term.
steps: The candidates are ±p/q, where p divides the CONSTANT term and q divides the LEADING coefficient.
The constant term here is −10, so p comes from 1, 2, 5 and 10.
The leading coefficient is 3, so q comes from 1 and 3.
Candidates are therefore factors of 10 over factors of 3.

ex.main: **Factors of 10 over factors of 3.** Getting this upside down is the single commonest slip in the whole theorem, and it is silent — the wrong list still looks like a list of fractions. A quick check: if the leading coefficient is 1, every candidate should be a whole number, which only works with the leading coefficient underneath.
ex.tip: Constant on top, leading coefficient underneath. Leading 1 means whole-number candidates.

questions.q: A polynomial with RATIONAL coefficients has degree 4, and two of its roots are 2 − √5 and i. What are the other two?
opts: −2 + √5 and −i
2 + √5 only — i does not need a partner
2 + √5 and −i
√5 − 2 and −i
questions.hint: Two different conjugate rules apply here, and each one pairs off exactly one of the given roots.
steps: Irrational roots of a rational polynomial come in pairs: 2 − √5 forces 2 + √5.
Non-real roots of a real polynomial come in pairs: i forces −i.
Only the sign on the radical or on the i flips — the rest of the number stays put.
So the other two roots are 2 + √5 and −i.

ex.main: **2 + √5 and −i.** Both conjugate rules are running at once, which is why this shape shows up on tests. Flipping the 2 as well gives −2 + √5, a different number entirely: the conjugate of a − √b is a + √b, changing only the sign in front of the radical.
ex.tip: Flip the sign on the radical, or on the i. Never on anything else.

questions.q: Which polynomial has 1 + i and 1 − i as its only roots?
opts: x² + 2
x² + 2x + 2
x² − 2x − 2
x² − 2x + 2
questions.hint: Multiply the two factors out — the i terms are meant to cancel.
steps: The factors are (x − (1 + i)) and (x − (1 − i)).
Their sum of roots is 2, so the middle term is −2x.
Their product is (1 + i)(1 − i) = 1 − i² = 2, so the constant is 2.
The polynomial is x² − 2x + 2.

ex.main: **x² − 2x + 2.** Building a polynomial from a conjugate pair is the reverse of finding roots, and it always lands on real coefficients — that is what the pairing is for. The product (1 + i)(1 − i) is 2 rather than 0, because i² = −1 makes the last term ADD rather than subtract.
ex.tip: Sum of roots → middle term (negated). Product of roots → constant.

questions.q: The Rational Root Theorem lists twelve candidates for a cubic with real coefficients, and testing shows none of them is a root. What does that tell you?
opts: It has no rational roots — its roots are irrational, non-real, or a mix
It has no roots at all, so there is nothing further to find
An arithmetic error was made, since every cubic has a rational root
All three of its roots are non-real, and none of them is real
questions.hint: The theorem only ever ruled on one kind of number.
steps: The theorem lists every POSSIBLE rational root and nothing else.
An empty result therefore rules out rational roots, and only rational roots.
Irrational roots like √2 and non-real roots like 2i were never on the list to begin with.
So the roots exist, but none of them is rational.

ex.main: **No rational roots — they are irrational, non-real, or both.** x³ − 2 is the plain example: its only real root is the cube root of 2, which no candidate list could ever contain. And a real cubic always has at least one real root, because its ends point opposite ways, so "all three non-real" is impossible whatever the candidates say.
ex.tip: An empty candidate list rules out rational roots. It rules out nothing else.

questions.q: P(x) = x³ + 2x² + 3x + 6. Find its one real root and say what the other two are.
opts: x = −2, and the other two are ±√3
x = −2, and the other two are ±i√3
x = 2, and the other two are ±i√3
x = −3, and the other two are ±i√2
questions.hint: Four terms with a shared structure — try grouping them in pairs.
steps: Group: x²(x + 2) + 3(x + 2).
Both pairs share (x + 2), so P(x) = (x + 2)(x² + 3).
x + 2 = 0 gives the real root x = −2.
x² + 3 = 0 gives x² = −3, so x = ±i√3.

ex.main: **x = −2, with ±i√3 as the other two.** Grouping is worth trying on any four-term cubic before reaching for the candidate list. The leftover x² + 3 has no real root, since squaring a real number never gives −3 — dropping the i and writing ±√3 is the slip to watch, and those are not roots of this polynomial at all.
ex.tip: Four terms → try grouping. x² = −k gives ±i√k, never ±√k.

questions.q: Why can a polynomial with real coefficients never have exactly ONE non-real root?
opts: Every root of a polynomial with real coefficients has to be real itself
The Fundamental Theorem of Algebra forbids non-real roots in a real polynomial
Non-real roots of a real polynomial arrive in conjugate pairs, so they come in twos
A polynomial with real coefficients always has an even degree
questions.hint: What would have to be true of the coefficients if a lone non-real root were allowed?
steps: If a + bi is a root of a real polynomial, so is a − bi.
The two are different numbers whenever b is not zero, so they are two separate roots.
Non-real roots therefore always come in twos and are even in number.
One on its own is impossible.

ex.main: **They come in conjugate pairs, so always in twos.** The pairing is what keeps the coefficients real when the factors are multiplied out — the i terms cancel, which they could not do without a partner. This is also why an odd-degree real polynomial must have a real root: an odd count cannot be made entirely of pairs.
ex.tip: Pairs cancel the i terms. A lone non-real root would leave one behind in the coefficients.

questions.q: A degree-5 polynomial with real coefficients has 2i, −2i and 1 + i among its roots. How many real roots does it have?
opts: It cannot be decided without knowing the leading coefficient of the polynomial
None — with four non-real roots the fifth must be non-real as well
Two — 1 − i is already one of the five listed, leaving two real ones
One — 1 − i must be a root too, so four are non-real and the fifth cannot be
questions.hint: One of the three given roots is still missing its partner. Add it in before you count.
steps: 1 + i is non-real, so its conjugate 1 − i must be a root as well.
2i and −2i are already a pair, so the non-real roots now number four.
Degree 5 means five roots in total, leaving exactly one unaccounted for.
A single leftover cannot be non-real, because it would need a partner of its own — so it is real.

ex.main: **Exactly one real root.** The counting argument is the point: non-real roots come in twos, so whatever is left over after the pairs must be real if it is odd in number. The leading coefficient scales the whole polynomial and moves no root at all, which is why it cannot affect the answer.
ex.tip: Pair everything off first. An odd leftover has to be real.

questions.q: A storage bin shaped like a rectangular prism measures x by x + 2 by x − 1 feet and holds 140 ft³. Which equation represents this, written as P(x) = 0?
questions.hint: Multiply the three sides out first, then get everything onto one side.
steps: Volume is the product: x(x + 2)(x − 1).
(x + 2)(x − 1) = x² + x − 2, so the product is x³ + x² − 2x.
Set that equal to 140: x³ + x² − 2x = 140.
Subtract 140 from both sides: x³ + x² − 2x − 140 = 0.

ex.main: **x³ + x² − 2x − 140 = 0.** Subtracting the volume across is what makes the Zero Product Property and the Rational Root Theorem available at all — both need a zero on one side. Watch the middle bracket: (x + 2)(x − 1) is x² + x − 2, and reading the minus as a plus gives x² + 3x + 2 and a wrong cubic that still looks plausible.
ex.tip: Multiply, then move the volume across. A volume problem is not solved until one side is 0.

questions.q: A crate measures x − 1 by x by x + 4 feet and holds 96 ft³. What are its dimensions?
opts: 4 ft by 5 ft by 9 ft
3 ft by 4 ft by 8 ft
2 ft by 3 ft by 7 ft
1 ft by 2 ft by 6 ft
questions.hint: Find x first, then work out what each expression comes to. Multiplying your answer back is the check.
steps: The volume gives x(x − 1)(x + 4) = 96, so x³ + 3x² − 4x − 96 = 0.
Testing candidates, x = 4 works: 64 + 48 − 16 − 96 = 0.
Substituting back: x − 1 = 3, x = 4 and x + 4 = 8.

ex.main: **3 ft by 4 ft by 8 ft.** Finding x = 4 is only most of the work — the question asks for the dimensions, and answering 4 is the commonest way to lose the mark. Multiplying the three back together takes a second and confirms the whole thing at once.
ex.tip: Solve for x, substitute into every side, then multiply back to check.

questions.q: Solving a crate’s volume gives x³ + 3x² − 4x − 96 = 0, which factors as (x − 4)(x² + 7x + 24). How many usable values of x are there, and how do you know?
opts: Two — x = 4, and one of the two roots of the quadratic factor
Three — every root of the cubic is a side length the box could have
One — x = 4; the quadratic’s discriminant is negative, so its roots are not real
None — a cubic cannot describe a real box in the first place
questions.hint: Check the discriminant of the quadratic before hunting for its roots.
steps: x − 4 = 0 gives the real root x = 4.
For x² + 7x + 24 the discriminant is 7² − 4(1)(24) = 49 − 96 = −47.
A negative discriminant means both of its roots are non-real.
A side length must be real and positive, so x = 4 is the only usable value.

ex.main: **One — x = 4, and the discriminant proves it.** Computing 49 − 96 = −47 settles the other two roots without ever finding them, which is the efficient move. They are perfectly good roots of the equation and completely useless as a measurement — the algebra answers a wider question than the box does.
ex.tip: A negative discriminant closes the question. You never have to work out roots you are going to reject.

questions.q: What are all the real and complex roots of x⁴ + 5x² − 36?
opts: 2, −2 and 3i only
4 and −9, from x² = 4 and x² = −9
questions.hint: It factors like a quadratic in x². Then take the square root of each part — including the negative one.
steps: Treat it as a quadratic in x²: it factors as (x² + 9)(x² − 4).
x² − 4 = 0 gives x = 2 and x = −2.
x² + 9 = 0 gives x² = −9, so x = 3i and x = −3i.
All four roots: 2, −2, 3i and −3i.

ex.main: **2, −2, 3i and −3i.** Answering 4 and −9 is the un-substitution trap: those are values of x², not of x. The x² + 9 factor is the interesting one — over the real numbers it does not factor at all, but with i available it contributes two perfectly good roots, and a degree-4 polynomial has to have four.
ex.tip: x² = −9 is not a dead end once i exists. It is 3i and −3i.
